sessions.title: 7 Ways You Can Build an Amazing Dev Career in the AI Era
sessions.description:
Are you also wondering where you fit in all of this?

Every day, you are bombarded with claims that AI will transform software development. Is this an unprecedented opportunity or an existential threat?

After more than 30 years in the software industry, I've seen technologies create opportunities, destroy opportunities, and completely reshape careers.

Yet... there are always professionals who seem to thrive regardless of the changes happening around them.

Why do some become more valuable... while others struggle?

In this interactive presentation, you'll face the myths around AI head-on and explore why some developers create more opportunities for themselves in the age of AI... while others are left afraid and scrambling to keep up.

You'll look beyond the headlines and discover the skills, behaviors, and decisions that continue to create opportunities... even during times of massive technological change.

Because the future may belong to those who understand something deeper than technology itself...

categoryItems.name: Soft Skills in an AI Era

sessions.title: Agentic Coding, Intentional Design
sessions.description:
AI coding agents are exceptionally good at producing working code.  Give a coding agent a feature request and a Quarkus project, and it will produce a working Java app.  However, working code doesn’t necessarily follow good design, and agents often produce code that ignores architectural boundaries and scatters business logic across an application’s layers.

Domain-Driven Design exists to manage complexity through explicit models and a shared language, isolating business logic and clearly implementing business rules.  DDD also provides critical structure and constraints for AI-generated code.  In this session, we explore how AI coding assistants can implement good design, allowing developers and architects to focus on the modeling decisions and business rules that define the system.

We’re going to build the same feature twice: once with only the requirements and once with repository Skills tailored for DDD and the Quarkus ecosystem.  We will dive into how bounded contexts, business rules, and separation of concerns can be encoded into persistent agentic guidance so that our architecture survives multiple conversations.

Attendees will leave with practical techniques for turning architecture into persistent agent guidance, structuring Skills for Java and Quarkus applications, and evaluating whether AI-generated code preserves the architecture they intended.

sessions.title: AI Says This Java Code Is Better. Let’s Check.
sessions.description:
An AI assistant suggests a Java refactoring. The explanation sounds convincing. The code compiles. The tests pass. Would you merge it?

Your experience with code reviews, debugging, testing, and Java APIs gives you a strong starting point for evaluating AI-generated code. This session shows how to put that knowledge to work and choose tools that help you check the recommendations.

Drawing on examples from BYLES, Germany’s largest digital reading screening platform for primary school children, we investigate what makes a proposed change worth applying. You will learn how to approach verification, choose useful tools, and understand what the results tell you. Understanding this process also helps you identify the verification work you can later ask an AI agent to carry out.

The approach is independent of any particular AI assistant, IDE, or vendor. You will leave with practical methods for deciding what needs checking, choosing suitable tools, and using the evidence to make an informed merge decision. Build on what you already know and apply it with the tools you prefer.

sessions.title: Autopilot: Building the Ultimate Ops Engineer with JFR and AI
sessions.description:
JDK Flight Recorder (JFR) is an observability and diagnostic framework built directly into the JDK. It can provide a rich and detailed view into how your application and the JVM are behaving at runtime. It is able to do this while maintaining a sub-1% impact on application throughput, allowing it to be always on in production.

While JFR is an incredibly powerful tool, its utilization is rather low, and the amount of information it provides can feel overwhelming. JFR can be always on, but the engineers needed to analyze its recordings can't be. And if an issue happens at 2:00 a.m., it might mean waiting hours before a human engineer can review the recording and offer a solution.

In this presentation, we will look at how JFR can be combined with agentic AI to build the ultimate Ops engineer: an engineer that can review JFR recordings and propose improvements to an application; an engineer that is always available, day and night, and able to respond in real time as issues occur.

If you have been looking for novel opportunities to incorporate AI into your organization or improve the performance of your applications in production, this is a presentation you don't want to miss.

sessions.title: Beyond LLMs: Hybrid AI Patterns for Real Applications
sessions.description:
Large language models have made it easier than ever to add AI capabilities to applications, but they are not a universal solution. In production systems, asking an LLM to do everything can lead to unnecessary cost, weaker control, and architectures that are harder to test and maintain. Many real applications work better when LLMs are combined with more traditional techniques such as rules, retrieval, scoring, search, or optimization.
This talk presents a practical, engineering-focused approach to hybrid AI design. We will look at where LLMs shine, where they struggle, and how to decide which parts of a system should remain deterministic or algorithmic. Rather than treating the model as the application, we will explore how to use it as one component within a broader architecture that may also include workflow logic, retrieval pipelines, classification, ranking, or search-based methods.
The goal is not to argue against LLMs, but to show how to use them more effectively by pairing them with the right supporting techniques. Attendees will leave with a clearer framework for choosing between LLM-driven behavior and classical approaches, along with practical design patterns for building AI-powered applications that are more reliable, maintainable, and production-ready.

Key takeaways
- How to identify which parts of an application are a good fit for LLMs and which are better handled by classical logic or algorithms.
- Practical patterns for combining LLMs with retrieval, rules, ranking, search, and workflow orchestration.
- A more disciplined architecture mindset for building AI-powered applications in production.

Target audience
Software developers, architects, tech leads, and AI engineers who want a practical framework for applying modern AI techniques without over-engineering or over-relying on LLMs.

sessions.title: Bootiful Security
sessions.description: It's not real until it's secure, and there's no better framework with which to secure your applications than Spring Security. Join me and we'll look at how Spring Security works, how to integrate it into your applications, and where you can scale out to secure your systems and services.

sessions.title: Break Your Java Agent Before Someone Else Does
sessions.description:
An AI agent follows instructions hidden in the content it reads. A poisoned document or a malicious tool result arrives as trusted input, and once MCP and tools grant the agent real privileges, a planted sentence can move money, delete data, or leak a key.

Prompt injection tops the OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications, and there is no one-size-fits-all fix for that: a model reads instructions and data as one input. The coding agent you work with every day has the same weakness, and it runs with access to your shell and your repository.

But there are defenses that hold for both, and I'll build them live: in LangChain4j for the agent you ship, and in the permission controls of the agent that writes code with you.

You will know the exact place in your agent, and in your coding workflow, where a planted instruction would land, and what to build there as a proper defense.

sessions.title: Context and Similarity - Food for Thought
sessions.description:
In GenAI Java applications, “context” is critically important for guiding LLMs to generate useful results.  You can include context in a simple prompt or extract it from a data store, e.g., in a RAG-based system. Context is what separates a chatbot that sounds smart from one that is actually helpful.  It lets agents make more accurate decisions about what actions to take.  Unfortunately, control of your context also allows black hats to distort results for nefarious purposes. 
This short session breaks down context into similarity and embeddings.  You’ll learn the fundamentals of embeddings, how embeddings turn text into vectors, how similarity search finds the best matching chunks, and what your Java code is really doing when it chunks documents, queries a vector store, and selects results to feed the LLM. We will cover the practical knobs that matter, including chunk size and overlap, metadata filters, distance metrics, and top-k settings, and how each one impacts answer quality, latency, and the risk of hallucinations. You will also see why adding more context and larger “context windows” isn't always better, and how to focus on the right context instead.

sessions.title: Customer Trust Is the Last Real Edge: A Leader's Guardrails for AI Adoption
sessions.description:
Every competitor has the same models. The differentiator is whether customers trust what you ship. A practical guide for leaders on setting AI guardrails, deciding what's actually ready, and protecting engineering quality while moving fast.

This session is about the decisions leaders own when AI enters the SDLC:
Where AI genuinely creates value in your delivery pipeline vs. where it quietly moves risk downstream
Setting guardrails teams will actually follow — and why blanket policies fail
Rebuilding the go/no-go decision for features whose behavior you can't fully specify
What to measure to know whether AI adoption is improving quality or just increasing throughput of rework
Helping senior engineers adapt without treating their skepticism as resistance

Grounded in real enterprise AI launch-readiness programs, including where the initial approach was wrong.

Target audience: Engineering managers, architects, technical program managers, senior ICs guiding AI adoption.

Takeaways:
A decision framework for where AI belongs in your SDLC
Guardrail patterns that survive contact with real teams
Leading indicators that distinguish quality improvement from rework growth
Level: Intermediate

sessions.title: DevOps Never Finished, And AI Is Exposing the Wall We Never Actually Tore Down
sessions.description:
In 2009, DevOps promised to tear down the wall between developers and operations. Sixteen years later, DORA's own research says only 19% of teams ever actually got there, and by 2025 the industry had to quietly retire its old scorecard because it had become measurement theater instead of a real signal.

Then AI showed up, and instead of closing the gap, it made the fragmentation worse. Teams are now losing close to a full workday per person, per week, wrangling AI tools that don't talk to the rest of the pipeline, and half of all enterprise AI agents are running in complete isolation from everything else.

This talk traces DevOps from its two-person origin story in an empty conference room to its current, mostly-ceremonial state, then makes the case for AI-Native Engineering (AINE) as the shift that actually finishes the job: rebuilding developer workflows, extending SDLC understanding past the dev team, and giving AI a system to amplify instead of a mess to accelerate.

sessions.title: Durable, composable and scalable agents with Spring AI 3.0
sessions.description:
Getting an LLM to call a few tools is the easy part. Running agents in production is harder: a multi-step agent will crash partway through, stop to wait for a human, hand work to other agents and stream tokens to thousands of users at once. Spring AI 3.0 adds a new spring-ai-agent module for these problems, built with the same type safety, extensibility and operational focus as the rest of the Spring portfolio.

This talk covers its key features:

Composable: an agent is a typed generic Agent transformation. You can build one from a ChatClient you already have, or from a graph whose nodes call the model and run tools. Graph agents can orchestrate nested agents. Their conversations can be shared, forked or isolated. Mismatched contexts are caught when the agent is built, not halfway through a run.

Durable: the durability feature snapshots each completed step, so a run that crashed picks up where it stopped instead of calling the LLM again. The same mechanism powers human-in-the-loop: interrupt nodes pause a run and resume it with the human's answer, even deep inside nested agents. For production-grade orchestration, nodes can also run as Temporal activities.

Observable and extensible: logging, conversation persistence and compaction, and durability are all pluggable features. Each one is written once on a single set of hooks and sees every model call, tool call and node, including those of nested agents.
Scalable: Spring AI 3.0 provide an innovative unified API with either a blocking call or an imperative event stream with backpressure designed for virtual threads and structured concurency, with no reactive programming required.

You'll leave knowing how to design agentic systems that are reliable, testable and ready for production, and how the new module fits into the Spring AI programming model.

sessions.title: Engineering Patterns for Building AI-native applications
sessions.description:
AI agents become much harder to engineer once they move beyond a single model call. This session explores practical patterns for building production-ready agentic applications, including orchestration strategies, managing what enters the context window, structuring model and tool calls, and recovering from partial failures.

We’ll look at how to design workflows that can retry safely, resume after interruptions, preserve the right state, and avoid unnecessary context and model usage. The focus is on concrete engineering patterns for building AI-native applications that are reliable, efficient, and maintainable in production.

sessions.title: Fix Production Rollouts on the Fly with Agentic AIOps
sessions.description:
Your software rollouts to production are probably always flawless, right? For the rest of us, once in a while we do run into issues when releasing code to production. Argo Rollouts is a great tool to help mitigate these issues by progressively delivering software to production, and automatically rolling back new features if anything doesn’t go right. 

Wouldn’t it be nice if we can take this functionality to the next level? We can take advantage of the advances made in Agentic AI (with Java!) and instruct a model to analyze the logs when a rollout fails. Then thanks to the use of agents, it can take action on our behalf, such as fixing the code or the deployment manifests on the fly, creating new PRs and sending notifications. The sky is really the limit. 

Come to this session to learn how to combine Argo Rollouts with Agentic AI to achieve the most seamless release experience yet.

sessions.title: Fundamentals of Software Engineering in the Age of AI
sessions.description:
AI doesn't replace what you know. It multiplies it. Hand a coding agent to someone who understands design, testing, and how systems fail, and they move faster than ever. Hand it to someone who doesn't, and they produce more code they can't explain, faster than ever. Same tool. Very different results.

That's what the "software engineering is dead" headlines miss. We've heard it before with code generators, low-code, and no-code. Each time, the job changed, the fundamentals stayed, and the people who understood the craft came out ahead.

In this keynote, Dan Vega and Nate Schutta look at what is really changing in our work and what is just noise. We'll talk about the skills that matter more now, not less: reading code critically, naming and design, testing, and the judgment to know when an answer is wrong. You'll leave knowing where to invest your time, and why the craft is worth more than ever.

categoryItems.name: Soft Skills in an AI Era

sessions.title: Generation Got Cheap. Your Review Budget Didn't.
sessions.description:
Teams adopting coding agents measure the wrong thing. Output goes up, so it looks like a win, and then the queue of unreviewed work grows, seniors become full-time reviewers, and quality erodes in a way that shows up two quarters later.

This is a talk about capacity planning when one half of the pipeline got ten times faster and the other half didn't: what to measure instead of lines or PR count, where to spend engineering effort on automated verification so humans aren't the throughput limit, and how to say no to velocity claims that don't survive contact with the review queue.

sessions.title: How to Build Auditable Memory Using Context Graphs
sessions.description:
Your AI agent just denied someone's loan application. Or it approved a $100K credit line increase. Or it rejected a prior authorization for medical treatment. Now you’re in court. And someone asks you to explain its decision. What are you going to say?  

In production, AI agents are making real decisions that impact real people's lives, and when those decisions get challenged by customers, compliance teams, auditors, or courts, you need answers.

This session will teach the best techniques to build AI agents that will pass an audit, using context graphs. Instead of black-box reasoning, you get complete decision traceability showing what information the agent considered, which factors influenced its choice, what alternatives it evaluated, and exactly how it reached its conclusion. I'll demo an AI agent evaluating a credit line increase request, then we'll trace the complete reasoning chain from input to output. We aren’t building this agent to simply explain itself (or hallucinate when explaining itself) after the fact. We are building it to capture decision-making as queryable graph structures, and get working code for building agents that can actually justify their decisions. So the next time anyone asks why your agent made that decision, you'll have a real answer.

sessions.title: Making the JVM Faster with AI: Promises and Pitfalls
sessions.description:
AI is radically changing the art of software development.  The most common use cases involve enhanced IDE autocompletion, tools like Claude Code and even the idea of Vibe coding entire applications.  This is, of course, targeted at traditional end-user or B2B type applications.  To date, AI has not been used much in lower-level systems programming and core infrastructure; in fact, OpenJDK explicitly bans the submission of AI-generated code.

At Azul, we have developed a high-performance JVM, based on OpenJDK, but with significant internal changes to deliver both lower latency and higher throughput.  Part of this is replacing the legacy C2 JIT compiler with one based on the open-source LLVM project.

In this session, we'll explore how we've been investigating (and making use of) optimisations identified and developed with AI tools such as Claude.  Although this has provided some interesting enhancements and overall speed improvements, we'll also discuss AI hallucinations claiming improvements that don't exist.

At the end, you'll have a clearer picture of how AI can be applied to less conventional areas of software development.

sessions.title: MCP Killed the Handshake: What Stateless Really Means for Agents
sessions.description:
Older MCP was stateless in spirit and stateful in practice: initialize opened a session, and every later message leaned on that memory. The 2026-07-28 revision removed the handshake outright. There is no first message, no session, and a server that needs input cannot send a request — modern clients silently discard them.

This talk walks the wire. Live in MCP Inspector we will watch discovery replace initialize, watch _meta replace the session, and watch a server ask a question by answering a tool call. Then: a tool that returns a UI, a task handle instead of a blocking result, and why continuation state now has to travel on the wire — because the server has nowhere else to keep it.

If you have only used an MCP SDK, this is the protocol underneath. If you are about to build a server, this is why “just add a session” is the wrong instinct.

sessions.title: Microservices in the GenAI Era
sessions.description:
The microservice architecture has traversed the hype cycle and is no longer as popular as it once was.
In part, there's been an unhealthy backlash to the hype and to poorly designed microservices.
But mostly, the industry has matured: organizations have learned to use the microservice architecture only when they suffer from the socio-technical problems it addresses.
Today, however, a new technology — also in the middle of its own hype cycle — is dramatically increasing the need for microservices: GenAI coding agents.

This two-part talk explores the surprising connection between GenAI and microservices.
In the first part, I explain why GenAI coding agents, by scaling software development, amplify the rate of change and create the very scaling pressures that the microservice architecture is designed to handle.
You will learn how to recognize the signals that indicate GenAI coding agents have caused you to outgrow your monolith.
In the second part, I show how GenAI can help you design a microservice architecture.
I demonstrate an AI-based assistant that guides you through the process.
You will learn how GenAI can accelerate the journey from monolith to a well-designed microservice architecture.

sessions.title: No Country For Old APIs. Wrapping legacy Java services as MCP tools without rewriting them.
sessions.description:
Somewhere in your estate is a Java service old enough to vote. REST endpoints by the dozen, one SOAP relic nobody will admit to, session auth, and the person who understood it all has retired. It works, which is why nobody touches it. And now the business wants AI agents to use it.

Every enterprise is under pressure to connect AI agents to systems that were never designed for them, yet most MCP material assumes a greenfield project or a toy demo. This session addresses the situation attendees actually face: a brownfield estate of REST and SOAP services that cannot be rewritten. It is demo-driven, built on the official MCP Java SDK, Spring AI, and Spring for GraphQL, and it is honest about the failure modes: tool sprawl from auto-generation, auth translation, oversized responses, and unsafe retries against non-idempotent writes.

Attendees leave with a reusable pattern set (facade first, curation over generation, read-only first, approval gates) they can apply to their own estate the following week.

sessions.title: Nobody Taught You How to Work With Humans
sessions.description:
We spend years teaching engineers how to work with computers. How to debug them, structure them, make them faster, and keep them from doing wildly unexpected things.

Then one day, the job quietly changes.

Suddenly, your biggest dependency is people.

And people have terrible documentation.

There’s no API. The error messages are vague. Production behavior is wildly inconsistent. And somehow, nobody thought this deserved a course.

As engineers become more senior, technical ability is still essential and being right isn’t enough anymore. Your impact increasingly depends on your ability to explain a technical problem to someone who isn’t technical, push back without becoming “the engineer who always says no,” disagree productively, communicate tradeoffs, influence decisions you don’t own, and figure out what someone is actually asking for.

In this session, we’ll explore the human skills that turn technical expertise into influence. We’ll look at how to translate, not dumb down, technical concepts for different audiences, how to challenge an idea while staying part of the solution, why curiosity is an underrated technical skill, and what happens when your impact starts being measured less by what you personally build and more by what you enable.

Because eventually, the hardest systems you’ll work on aren’t written in Python, C#, JavaScript, or PHP.

They’re made of people.

categoryItems.name: Soft Skills in an AI Era

sessions.title: OK, But What About Predictive AI?
sessions.description:
While the tech world is buzzing about generative AI and large language models (LLMs), it's easy to forget that predictive AI has been, and continues to be, the real engine behind most AI-powered applications. From fraud detection to demand forecasting, predictive models are embedded in nearly every industry.

This talk takes a fresh look at the state of predictive AI in the Java ecosystem. We'll explore how traditional machine learning is still very much alive, practical, and evolving, especially with recent improvements in model efficiency, portability, and tooling.

You'll see real-world examples of predictive AI in action and discover some of the Java libraries, frameworks, and platforms that make it all work, from model training to serving. Whether you're new to AI or looking to balance your GenAI hype with some grounded, production-ready solutions, this session will reconnect you with the part of AI that’s still doing the heavy lifting.

sessions.title: Pouring AI Sauce on Your Architecture
sessions.description:
Today, you are being besieged by people claiming that AI is the secret ingredient that will solve every problem in your company. But AI is the sauce, not the meal—don’t let it drown your systems. There is tremendous business pressure to introduce AI into all aspects of your organization; however, many stakeholders, division leads, and developers lack a consistent understanding of what that truly means or a unified approach for assembling these pieces into a coherent system.
As architects, we must navigate the pros and cons to create architectures that solve business needs both today and in the future. We must also guide each of these groups toward building effective solutions. AI impacts your entire software development lifecycle, altering how you design, build, and test systems. As an architect, you need to design systems that take advantage of AI while limiting the blast radius of its approximations.  In an AI world, the fundamentals of software engineering, the practices, the discipline, the ceremonies, are *more* critical today as AI enables us to move faster with higher quality.

sessions.title: Refactoring LOL (Lean On LLMs)
sessions.description:
Refactoring LOL (Lean On LLMs)
Github copilot first came out in 2021 and The frontier models have only gotten better since then. In this age of AI and other powerful tools why should a developer take the time to learn manual refactoring? Or even plan and execute their own novel refactorings? 

This talk will delve into these questions with techniques for refactoring planning and humor. 

The audience for this session are software developers and the people that interface with them (product owners, scrum masters, development managers) who need to know the value of this important and often neglected technical practice.
 
At the end of the session, the attendee will be able to identify hidden patterns in their code bases, plan a refactor effort on legacy codebases, write their own refactorings, write skills files to help the AI do the refactoring, and know when to use AI or other tools to perform the refactoring.

sessions.title: Reinventing Testing Practices in the AI Era
sessions.description:
AI-infused applications demand a rethinking of our testing practices. Developers face a new class of challenge as LLMs become standard integration points in modern applications: non-deterministic behavior that traditional testing approaches were never designed to handle. The current wave of distributed, orchestrated, agentic AI systems is evolving fast and, if we're being honest, it smells a lot like the early days of microservices.

In this session, we'll explore how your DevOps and testing practices must evolve when you wire AI into your applications. Not all AI failures look the same, and recognizing the difference is the first step toward building systems you can actually trust. We'll walk through practical testing and observability strategies, using open source tools that give you confidence in AI-infused applications at every layer of the stack.

You'll leave with a concrete mental model for reasoning about AI failures and one grounding question: What if AI was just an API call?

sessions.title: Restoring Lost Work in Git: A Forbidden Love Story
sessions.description:
For a long time, I've said git is writing fan fiction when you're merging and rebasing. git loves fan fiction so much that it'll even invite you to help - like when you interactive rebase.

...so I wrote a piece of fan fiction about git.

Using this forbidden love story, I'll show that you should love refs and the reflog. We'll talk about how to set yourself up for success and find lost changes. You'll become comfortable with multiple to restore lost work.

Most importantly, you'll walk away confident that git loves you.

sessions.title: RoboCoders Judgement Day: From Side Projects to Software Factories
sessions.description:
Baruch and Viktor could vibecode an app live on stage. In fact, that was their shtick for many years. But in 2027, watching two people prompt a coding agent is about as impressive as watching
  them use autocomplete. Stopping when the app appears to work would also demonstrate the development practice they came to argue against.

  Instead, they're bringing stories from projects that survived their first demo and had to face the proverbial "Day 2". They'll open the projects, inspect the agent instructions and workflows,
  and question each other's fixes.

  Everybody says "demos are easy, production is hard", but what does that really mean? Viktor and Baruch will discuss familiar problems, like how an architectural decision disappears with the
  agent's conversation or how the next project needs the same coding rules. Then there's the swarm of agents, which apparently needs coordinating much like the team of software engineers it was
  supposed to replace. Can all of this be fixed? And what if each improvement moves the bottleneck somewhere else? Goldratt would recognize this factory.

  And then the factory meets the enterprise, and things really get out of hand. Shipping something now means finding who owns the service and what else depends on it, and all that information is
  scattered across ten different services, hostile to AI with prejudice. Can this hot spaghetti mess become usable by coding agents, starting with ownership and dependencies they can query? And
  perhaps the human in the loop, put there because compliance required one, could get enough context to make a decision without serving as a rubber-stamping meat proxy. The speakers will open
  the workflows they've built to try.

  Did AI solve coding? Maybe. Did AI solve software engineering? Not even close. Can we do better software engineering with AI? By the end of this session, you will be the judge.

sessions.title: Slopless in Atlanta: Six Steps to Agent Pull Requests That Maintainers Actually Merge
sessions.description:
Any codebase you depend on is now yours to fix, even in a language you don't write. The problem is that maintainers are drowning in sloppy pull requests blasted at them from other people's clankers. This talk is a method for contributing to any software project using coding agents without producing slop, shown on one rather nasty real bug. You can run the same steps on the next bug in your own codebase.

Handy is the open-source dictation app I use to talk to my agents, with 31,000 stars on GitHub. Its memory grew from 249 MB to 9.5 GB in 36 hours and the kernel killed my machine mid-sentence. The backend is 40,000 lines of Rust, a language I don't write. Someone else's agent-written fix didn't compile. Mine was merged. The difference was the engineering methodology I led the agents with:

1. **Give the agents a way to run the app.** A harness that runs it without me, including a way for an agent to speak into the microphone.
2. **Record every layer at once.** No one tool could see across the process boundaries the leak crossed, so the agents built one.
3. **Measure, don't guess.** Eight possible causes. The measurements cleared seven.
4. **Treat each fix as an experiment.** Three candidates, each behind a switch. One did nothing and was deleted.
5. **Have agents who know nothing review it cold.** They showed the headline metric hid most of the leak. The fix was a big reduction, not a cure.
6. **Ship the proof with the patch.** -2 MB over four hours against +3,885 MB without it.

None of this is specific to Rust, memory leaks, or open source. I'll show the whole arc, from the machine dying to the merge, and explain what I'd do differently next time. The full write-up is at gallon.me. Point your agent at it and it will know how to fix a bug this way.

sessions.title: Someone Vibe-Coded It. Now It's Your Problem.
sessions.description:
Non-developers are shipping working software now. A marketing lead builds an internal tool over a weekend, a founder ships a prototype that gets customers, a researcher writes the script the whole lab depends on. Then the tool has to be dependable, and someone has to make it so. That someone is increasingly going to be you, and the job is not "rewrite it." The job is to move it up a scale without losing what already works.

I think of projects as doghouses, cabins, and skyscrapers. A doghouse is small, casual, and shipped in a weekend, which is the vibe coding sweet spot. A cabin is modest but dependable, with a testable core and explicit boundaries. A skyscraper adds coordination, review gates, and CI discipline because other people have to work inside it. Most inherited vibe-coded projects need to become cabins, and the mistake in both directions is expensive. Build a doghouse like a skyscraper and you never finish. Run a skyscraper like a doghouse and it fails in ways that cost real money.

This session walks the doghouse-to-cabin transition on two real projects using Claude Code. A single-file JavaScript app that a request for tests forces into a testable core with boring DOM glue. A Spring Boot certificate service that started as a joke and ended with property-based tests on its cryptography. Along the way we do the read-only orientation pass that makes the agent mark where it is guessing, write the project memory that stops the next session from re-learning everything, decide what actually needs a test, and catch the failures that come with the territory. Tests the agent rewrote until they passed. A confident architecture map that disagreed with the code. A refactor that quietly changed behavior.

You'll leave with a triage sequence for any inherited agent-written codebase, the prompts that drive each step, a rule for knowing when to stop, and a public repository showing both projects before and after.

sessions.title: Spend Your Tokens Where They Matter: Development with a Token Budget
sessions.description:
You want to use AI to do all the things. Maybe you did. You were feeling like a rockstar. Then you were told you have a $300 monthly limit. Now what?

When your token budget is fixed, you have to be more judicious about where you spend it. Some fancy techniques simply will not fit. This talk explores practical ways to structure AI assisted development, choose where model effort is worthwhile, and make room for research, implementation, and review within a real budget. A custom workflow based on Dexter Horthy’s “Everything We Got Wrong About Research Plan Implement” provides a running example.

sessions.title: Taming the Chaos: Security and Predictability in LLM-Powered Applications
sessions.description:
LLMs are probabilistic by nature. Ask the same question twice, get different answers. Great for creativity, terrible for business logic. How do you build reliable systems on top of something inherently unreliable?

Let's tackle this together – from security to predictability. We'll look at guardrails that block prompt injection and redact leaked PII before it leaves your system. Then we'll layer on deterministic validation that catches hallucinations with code, not hope. And when the model gets it wrong, we'll feed errors back for self-correction and use multi-model consensus to build confidence. Practical patterns, real code, no magic.

This isn't about making LLMs perfect – it's about building systems that fail safely and predictably when they're not.

The examples are in Java and LangChain4J; the concepts – transferable to other languages and frameworks.

sessions.title: Testing Java apps in the age of AI
sessions.description:
How do you know the code that AI wrote works? How do you know the tests the AI wrote work? How do you know the code does what you want? Testing has changed over the last few years and adapting the mindset of how to test with it.

While AI can generate code quickly, that doesn’t mean it is correct. After all humans write buggy code too! 

In this session, you’ll learn techniques for improving tests for new and existing code and how to get ore thorough tests. You’ll see how to use tools like code coverage and mutation testing to see how thorough they are. You’ll also see examples of how to tell if the work is even correct. After all, having a regression test for an AI generated bug still leaves you with the bug.

sessions.title: The Demo Worked. Then Reality Happened: Building AI Inference for the Real World
sessions.description:
Getting an AI model to answer a prompt is the easy part. Keeping it useful when multiple users, multi-gigabyte models, limited GPUs and real infrastructure enter the picture is where the engineering begins.

This talk follows the evolution of a small three-GPU AI lab from “we have some spare hardware, let’s run some models” into a shared inference platform used by a development team, including the failures that shaped it along the way.

We’ll look at what happened when parallel model downloads overwhelmed the network, how fixing one bottleneck exposed the next, and why more GPUs didn’t make problems around model distribution, resource allocation, observability and recovery disappear. We’ll also explore the guardrails needed when an experiment becomes infrastructure that other developers depend on for day-to-day inference.

Then the models got bigger.

As the lab moves from text models toward multimodal inference, local hardware is no longer always enough. We’ll look at the next challenge: extending the same platform onto temporary high-end GPU infrastructure without turning startup time, model caching and cloud costs into the new bottlenecks.

Using OpenShift, Kubernetes, vLLM and the surrounding inference ecosystem, we’ll examine what it really takes to move from “the demo works” to AI infrastructure people can actually rely on.

Attendees will leave with practical patterns for shared inference, model distribution, observability and resource management and a better sense of which AI infrastructure problems more GPUs simply won’t solve.

sessions.title: The Human API: DevOps for the Soul
sessions.description: Between the pace of change and the demands of modern software, many engineers are struggling to keep their heads above water. From burnout to imposter syndrome, more often than not, we treat our production environments with more respect than we do the people that build them. While it may seem like the answer to overload is to work more hours, skimp on sleep and throw self care overboard, work life balance is vital to successful projects. In this talk, you’ll learn how to learn without becoming overwhelmed, the importance of taking care of your core infrastructure and how to optimize your habits.

categoryItems.name: Soft Skills in an AI Era

sessions.title: The Secret You Encrypt Today Is Already Broken: Post-Quantum Cryptography for Every Developer
sessions.description:
Somewhere, a machine is being built that computes by letting possibilities interfere with one another, and in 1994 Peter Shor showed that such a machine could unravel the RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography protecting almost every connection your code makes. That machine does not yet exist at scale. It does not need to. Adversaries are already harvesting encrypted traffic today in order to decrypt it tomorrow, which means that anything your application sends that must stay secret for a decade is, in a meaningful sense, already exposed.

This session takes quantum computing out of the physics lab and puts it into your pull requests. Starting from an intuitive, equation-light tour of why quantum computers break today's cryptography, it moves to the practical answer: post-quantum cryptography. Attendees will see the NIST standards ML-KEM and ML-DSA, the post-quantum APIs already available in the JDK, hybrid key exchange already running in modern TLS, and the crypto-agility patterns that let systems change algorithms without rewrites. Drawing on the EU Q-FENCE project and a portfolio of quantum computing patents, the session closes with a migration checklist: find your cryptography, rank it by secrecy lifetime, and start moving.

sessions.title: The UX of AI: Making AI-Powered Apps Your Users Don't Hate
sessions.description:
As a developer, AI is fun, exciting, and full of potential – but users don't always feel the same way about it. 

From a UX perspective, AI comes with a whole new set of considerations around user trust, privacy, and security. From a UI perspective, AI brings new interaction patterns, new icons, new visual cues, and so much more! 

If we want people to get the most from what we build, we have to teach our users how to use AI. Let's look at ways to introduce new capabilities in our apps and guide our users through new patterns and processes – ideally without making them throw their phone out a window.

sessions.title: Think Fast: OnDevice AI and Vector Features
sessions.description: Did you know a phone could do that? Integrate on-device AI qualities into your React Native apps. The future is real-time, offline intelligence. In this session, we'll explore providing contextual information, all without relying on the cloud.

sessions.title: To Java 28 and Beyond!
sessions.description:
The Java release train has no brakes! Java 28 has arrived, and with it comes a whole set of new features and goodies!

In this presentation, we will start with a quick review of the key changes from JDK 17 through JDK 25 and how they have improved the developer experience, performance, and support for Java applications in production.

From there, we will transition to changes in Java post-JDK 25 and how they are bringing several important stories into focus, including improved concurrency support, data-oriented programming, native support, and more!

The Java platform is evolving quickly to keep pace with the current needs of its users. Be sure to attend this presentation if you want to keep up!

sessions.title: Toxic Flows in MCP Servers and Skills: What Your Agent Blindly Trusts
sessions.description:
AI agents don't just trust MCP servers. They trust Skills too. Both are attack surfaces, yet most teams treat neither as part of the same trust model.

In this talk, we introduce toxic flows: trust paths through an agent stack where tool descriptions, MCP responses, and Skill definitions can leak sensitive context, manipulate agent decisions, and trigger unintended actions without the model violating a single instruction. We demonstrate this live.

This session is not about adding authentication or wrapping everything in TLS. It's about understanding how trust failures emerge, how they mirror familiar software risks like dependency confusion and unsafe deserialization, and how to design MCP servers and Skill integrations that reduce trust, contain blast radius, and keep agent systems defensible.

Attendees will leave with a practical framework for identifying trust boundaries, evaluating agent integrations, and hardening their AI stack against toxic flows.

sessions.title: Traditional software development roles are collapsing - are you ready?
sessions.description:
Is your current role one of these - Front-end Engineer? Back-end Engineer? Android Developer? Java Developer? iOS Developer? Web developer? QA Engineer? Product Owner? Manager? Project Manager? Architect?  Security Engineer? UX Designer? Data Modeler?

Do you think, in the AI age they will continue to exist?

Of course these roles remain important but, as a "Builder" of software-intensive systems, you will probably have to absorb many of these roles previously performed by your peers on a typical software team. The scope of your work will most likely increase. 

You may be called up to deliver large projects by yourself (with AI assistance) what previously could only be achieved by a team of specialist (human) experts.

Learn from a real-world case study where I had to plan for and deliver a major project (replace identity management for our product).. solo.

sessions.title: Unlocking AI: Breaking the Safeguards in Open-Weight Models
sessions.description:
Model creators bake safety alignment into open weight models because they do not want to release a personalized Anarchist Cookbook, creating foreseeable harm, public backlash, and legal exposure. Many users want something different: capable models with fewer refusals, fewer restrictions, and less control retained by the developer.

Once the weights are downloaded, who gets the final say?

This talk follows the craft of model lockpicking. Researchers have shown that refusal behavior is not an unchangeable property of a model. It is produced by internal mechanisms that can be identified, weakened, and sometimes removed while much of the capability remains intact.

We will explore the latest research in modifying models to provide less push back or refusals for safety-aligned prompts and what the trade-offs are between refusal reduction and model accuracy.

This is not another prompt jailbreaking talk. Prompt attacks try to persuade a model to bend its rules. Model lockpicking changes the model itself.

Come see how we in the model-cracking community play a cat and mouse game with open weight model makers today, and why safety aligned may describe only the model as it left the factory.

sessions.title: What’s that? How an Agent & Context Graph analyzed a message stream
sessions.description:
Message streams are the backbone of information flow; from system logs and customer call histories to my message group with my oldest friends.

Communication, messaging, and memory is a complicated place. How are you supposed to make sense of it all?

In this hands-on talk, you will see how I used graphs and AI to summarise the complex streams of messages I get in my odd titled friends WhatsApp group.

sessions.title: When Garbage Collection Becomes an Availability Incident
sessions.description:
Abstract: 

Garbage collection is supposed to be invisible, the JVM quietly cleaning up while your service does the real work. Until the day it isn't.

When our production Java service's dataset grew 10x almost overnight, GC stopped being a latency nuisance and became an availability incident. Hosts started shedding live write traffic. Heap dumps told a surprising story. And some of the worst culprits were hiding in places no one thought to look.

This talk is the story of how we brought that service back from the edge, from JVM flags all the way down to the JDK itself. You'll see how to find what's really driving GC pressure, why the metric most teams chase is the wrong one, and which fixes paid off far more than expected. Walk away with a practical playbook for the day GC becomes your outage.


Elevator Pitch:

This talk is based on a real production incident I led the resolution of at LinkedIn. A Java metadata service's dataset grew 11x (17K to 200K+ records per region), and GC pressure escalated until host-level overload protection began dropping live write traffic. Heap dumps showed 93% of the heap was garbage.

The talk covers the full diagnosis and fix: JFR and heap-dump analysis, G1 humongous objects forcing mixed GCs, a 1GB+ framework header cache (over 40% of used heap), per-request object re-materialization fixed with identity-based caching, replacing a memory-heavy JSON library, OOM kills traced to native memory fragmentation and fixed with an allocator switch, and a major JDK upgrade.

Results: GC overload events and dropped-traffic incidents went to zero, peak GC health score rose from ~10 to 90+, and the JDK upgrade alone cut total GC pause time ~24% and p99 latency ~42%.

Attendees leave with a multi step, battle-tested playbook for treating GC as an availability concern rather than a tuning exercise. The talk is aimed at intermediate-to-advanced Java developers and SREs running data-heavy services.

sessions.title: You May Now Optimize The Wedding! An intro to Planning AI
sessions.description:
Every developer has been there: sitting at an important life event, thinking 'could I automate this?'. The answer is YES, and this talk will show you how.

There is a whole class of problems that GenAI alone cannot solve: scheduling, routing and planning challenges where every decision affects every other decision. Timefold tackles these in production every day, across logistics, manufacturing, healthcare, and yes, apparently also weddings.
  
We will use the most important weekend of your life as our excuse to explore constraint optimization in practice, from seating charts to pub crawls to honeymoon itineraries, with real code, real constraints and real solver magic. 
  
You'll leave knowing how to turn any 'could I automate this?' moment into a working optimization solution.

sessions.title: Your Agents Don't Need More Context. They Need True Context — and You Can't Buy It
sessions.description: Your agents have read every doc in the company. Nobody told them which ones are still true. At the enterprise level, the hard part isn't how much context agents get. It's the business rules and decisions that live in people's heads and stale or contradictory documents. This session walks through a seven-layer architecture for true context: how to collect, process, curate, and serve it. Context on your own machine only has to work for you. Once it serves a project or an organization, it needs to be curated continuously and keeps evolving. Some of those layers you can buy. Some you can't buy your way out of.

sessions.title: Your AI Can Design. You Still Have to Review It.
sessions.description:
In 2018, Angel gave a Devnexus talk called "When Developers Must Become Designers." The premise was simple: if there's no designer on your team, you need enough UX knowledge to recognize what works, what doesn't, and why.

Nine years later, it's the same problem with a new cause: AI can generate the interface for you. Describe a screen, get a polished UI, ship it. Vibe coding has made skipping the design process easier than ever.

But a finished-looking interface can hide unfinished thinking. AI can know your design system, follow your standards, and understand UX principles, and still make bad UX decisions. We already review generated code for exactly that reason. Most teams aren't reviewing the generated experience.

The failures are surprisingly predictable. AI builds the screen you described instead of the one the user needed. It handles the happy path you mentioned and misses the edge cases you didn't. It produces something coherent in isolation that falls apart when real data, real users, and real mistakes show up.

We'll give you a practical way to review AI-generated interfaces without becoming a UX designer. We'll look at the UX principles generated interfaces most reliably break, walk through a 10-minute review you can use on your next AI-built screen, and learn to separate subjective design preferences from actual usability problems.

The tools changed. The need to recognize bad UX didn't.

sessions.title: Your AI Maturity Score Is Probably Wrong
sessions.description:
Your organization has AI coding tools. Your developers use them every day. You may have an AI strategy, a governance program, and a growing list of AI projects. Does this make your organization AI mature?
Most organizations measure what is easy to count: licenses, adoption rates, generated code, and reported hours saved. These metrics show that developers use AI. They do not show that the organization builds better software with AI. 
This talk compares the major AI maturity models from CMU/SEI, DORA, NIST, and OWASP. We will show what each model measures, where the models overlap, and where they fail. Then we will discuss a practical framework that answers three questions:
Adoption: Do we use AI?
Capability: Do we have the engineering practices to use AI well?
Outcomes: Can we prove that AI improves delivery speed, quality, security, or developer experience?
You will see why high adoption often hides low maturity, why individual productivity metrics mislead leaders, and what to measure instead. The goal isn’t another five-level AI maturity staircase. It’s a way to gather evidence that an organization is actually getting better at building software in an AI-enabled world.

sessions.title: Your GPU, Your Model: Running Open-Weight AI
sessions.description:
Tired of cloud API latency, rate limits, and per-token bills? Open-weight models have gotten good enough, and runtimes fast enough, that your workstation can do real work. This session covers how to run, quantize, and serve open-weight models on your own hardware, and where the limits are.
We'll start with what a model actually is (weights, parameters, tokens) and why running it locally makes sense (or doesn't). Then we'll get practical:
Quantization: choosing a method and bit width for your memory budget, and what you give up
Inference engines: picking and configuring the right runtime for your hardware and use case
Hardware sizing: rules of thumb for memory bandwidth, VRAM, and context window management on local silicon
You'll leave knowing what your machine can realistically run, how fast, and when the cloud is still the better call. Bring your questions.
